concepts.def: Saying a word/phrase again in unplanned talk
Hesitations and pauses in real speech

walkthroughs.body_html: Unlike writing, talk has fillers, restarts and pauses — and that's totally normal.

Fillers: 'um', 'er', 'erm', 'like'.

False start: 'I was going to — well, actually I went.'

These give us thinking time.

'Right, so anyway.' — these little words flag a topic change, opening or closing.

They're the traffic signs of conversation.

mcqs.q: 'I went to — actually no, I stayed in' is an example of a:

options: A noun is any word that starts with a capital letter.
Phonemes are vowels and graphemes are consonants.
A noun is always a person, place or thing.
By the word's grammatical function in a sentence — not its meaning. The same word can belong to different classes depending on use (e.g. 'run' as noun or verb).

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a phoneme and a grapheme?
options: Phonemes are vowels and graphemes are consonants.
A noun is any word that starts with a capital letter.
Phonemes are letters and graphemes are syllables.
A phoneme is the smallest unit of sound in a language; a grapheme is the written letter or letters that represent it.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a dialect and an accent?
options: Dialect and accent mean the same thing.
Phonemes are vowels and graphemes are consonants.
Accent refers only to pronunciation; dialect includes vocabulary and grammar as well as pronunciation — so all dialects involve accents but not vice versa.
A dialect is a foreign language; an accent is how locals speak.
